mn2:1.2: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
mn2:1.3: There the Blessed One addressed the monks:
mn2:1.5: “Venerable sir!” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
mn2:2.1: “Monks, I will teach you the method for restraining all influxes.
mn2:2.2: Listen to it, pay close attention, and I will speak.”
mn2:2.3: “Yes, sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
mn2:3.1: “Monks, I say that the destruction of influxes is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see.
mn2:3.2: And what, monks, do I say is the destruction of influxes for one who knows and sees?
mn2:3.4: Monks, when one attends unwisely, unarisen influxes arise, and arisen influxes increase;
mn2:3.5: but when one attends wisely, unarisen influxes do not arise, and arisen influxes are abandoned.
mn2:4.1: Monks, there are influxes to be abandoned by seeing, influxes to be abandoned by restraint, influxes to be abandoned by use, influxes to be abandoned by endurance, influxes to be abandoned by avoidance, influxes to be abandoned by removal, and influxes to be abandoned by development.
mn2:5.0: 1. Influxes to Be Abandoned by Seeing
mn2:5.1: And what, monks, are the influxes to be abandoned by seeing?
mn2:5.2: Here, monks, an uninstructed ordinary person—who has not seen the noble ones, is unskilled in the teaching of the noble ones, untrained in the teaching of the noble ones, who has not seen good persons, is unskilled in the teaching of good persons, untrained in the teaching of good persons—
mn2:5.3: does not know the things worthy of attention or the things unworthy of attention.
mn2:5.4: Not knowing the things worthy of attention or unworthy of attention, they attend to things unworthy of attention and do not attend to things worthy of attention.
mn2:6.1: And what, monks, are the things unworthy of attention that they attend to?
mn2:6.2: Monks, when they attend to certain things, either an unarisen influx of sensual desire arises, or an arisen influx of sensual desire increases;
mn2:6.3: an unarisen influx of existence arises, or an arisen influx of existence increases;
mn2:6.4: an unarisen influx of ignorance arises, or an arisen influx of ignorance increases—
mn2:6.5: these are the things unworthy of attention that they attend to.
mn2:6.6: And what, monks, are the things worthy of attention that they do not attend to?
mn2:6.7: Monks, when they attend to certain things, an unarisen influx of sensual desire does not arise, or an arisen influx of sensual desire is abandoned;
mn2:6.8: an unarisen influx of existence does not arise, or an arisen influx of existence is abandoned;
mn2:6.9: an unarisen influx of ignorance does not arise, or an arisen influx of ignorance is abandoned—
mn2:6.10: these are the things worthy of attention that they do not attend to.
mn2:7.1: By attending to things unworthy of attention and not attending to things worthy of attention, unarisen influxes arise, and arisen influxes increase.
mn2:7.2: They attend unwisely in this way:
mn2:7.3: ‘Was I in the past? Was I not in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what did I become in the past?
mn2:7.4: Will I be in the future? Will I not be in the future? What will I be in the future? How will I be in the future? Having been what, what will I become in the future?’
mn2:7.5: Or they are inwardly perplexed about the present:
mn2:7.6: ‘Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? Where has this being come from? Where will it go?’
mn2:8.1: When they attend unwisely in this way, one of these six views arises in them.
mn2:8.2: The view ‘I have a self’ arises in them as true and established;
mn2:8.3: or the view ‘I have no self’ arises in them as true and established;
mn2:8.4: or the view ‘I perceive self with self’ arises in them as true and established;
mn2:8.5: or the view ‘I perceive not-self with self’ arises in them as true and established;
mn2:8.6: or the view ‘I perceive self with not-self’ arises in them as true and established;
mn2:8.7: or else they have this view:
mn2:8.8: ‘This self of mine that speaks and feels, that experiences the results of good and bad actions here and there—this self is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same forever.’
mn2:8.9: This, monks, is called a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a contortion of views, a vacillation of views, a fetter of views.
mn2:8.10: Bound by the fetter of views, monks, the uninstructed ordinary person is not freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair;
mn2:8.11: I say they are not freed from suffering.
mn2:9.2: who has seen the noble ones, is skilled in the teaching of the noble ones, well-trained in the teaching of the noble ones, who has seen good persons, is skilled in the teaching of good persons, well-trained in the teaching of good persons—
mn2:9.3: knows the things worthy of attention and the things unworthy of attention.
mn2:9.4: Knowing the things worthy of attention and unworthy of attention, they do not attend to things unworthy of attention and attend to things worthy of attention.
mn2:10.1: And what, monks, are the things unworthy of attention that they do not attend to?
mn2:10.2: Monks, when they attend to certain things, an unarisen influx of sensual desire arises, or an arisen influx of sensual desire increases;
mn2:10.3: an unarisen influx of existence arises, or an arisen influx of existence increases;
mn2:10.4: an unarisen influx of ignorance arises, or an arisen influx of ignorance increases—
mn2:10.5: these are the things unworthy of attention that they do not attend to.
mn2:10.6: And what, monks, are the things worthy of attention that they attend to?
mn2:10.7: Monks, when they attend to certain things, an unarisen influx of sensual desire does not arise, or an arisen influx of sensual desire is abandoned;
mn2:10.8: an unarisen influx of existence does not arise, or an arisen influx of existence is abandoned;
mn2:10.9: an unarisen influx of ignorance does not arise, or an arisen influx of ignorance is abandoned—
mn2:10.10: these are the things worthy of attention that they attend to.
mn2:10.11: By not attending to things unworthy of attention and attending to things worthy of attention, unarisen influxes do not arise, and arisen influxes are abandoned.
mn2:11.1: They attend wisely: ‘This is suffering,’ they attend wisely: ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ they attend wisely: ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ they attend wisely: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’
mn2:11.2: By attending wisely in this way, three fetters are abandoned in them—
mn2:11.3: the view of personal identity, doubt, and attachment to rites and rituals.
mn2:11.4: These, monks, are called the influxes to be abandoned by seeing.
mn2:12.0: 2. Influxes to Be Abandoned by Restraint
mn2:12.1: And what, monks, are the influxes to be abandoned by restraint?
mn2:12.2: Here, monks, a monk, reflecting wisely, dwells restrained with the restraint of the eye faculty.
mn2:12.3: If he dwelt unrestrained with the restraint of the eye faculty, influxes causing affliction and vexation would arise; but dwelling restrained with the restraint of the eye faculty, those influxes causing affliction and vexation do not arise.
mn2:12.4: Reflecting wisely, he dwells restrained with the restraint of the ear faculty …
mn2:12.5: restrained with the restraint of the nose faculty …
mn2:12.6: restrained with the restraint of the tongue faculty …
mn2:12.7: restrained with the restraint of the body faculty …
mn2:12.8: restrained with the restraint of the mind faculty.
mn2:12.9: If he dwelt unrestrained with the restraint of the mind faculty, influxes causing affliction and vexation would arise; but dwelling restrained with the restraint of the mind faculty, those influxes causing affliction and vexation do not arise.
mn2:12.10: If he dwelt unrestrained with restraint, influxes causing affliction and vexation would arise; but dwelling restrained with restraint, those influxes causing affliction and vexation do not arise.
mn2:12.11: These, monks, are called the influxes to be abandoned by restraint.
mn2:13.0: 3. Influxes to Be Abandoned by Use
mn2:13.1: And what, monks, are the influxes to be abandoned by use?
mn2:13.2: Here, monks, a monk, reflecting wisely, uses the robe:
mn2:13.3: ‘Only for protection from cold, protection from heat, protection from contact with flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping creatures, and only for the purpose of covering the private parts out of modesty.’
mn2:14.2: ‘Not for amusement, not for intoxication, not for adornment, not for beautification, but only for the sustenance and maintenance of this body, for ending discomfort, and for supporting the holy life, thinking: “Thus I will end old feelings without arousing new feelings, and I will be healthy, blameless, and live at ease.”’
mn2:15.2: ‘Only for protection from cold, protection from heat, protection from contact with flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping creatures, and only for the purpose of warding off the perils of the weather and enjoying seclusion.’
mn2:16.1: Reflecting wisely, he uses medicinal requisites for the sick:
mn2:16.2: ‘Only for protection from arisen painful feelings and for the sake of maximum freedom from affliction.’
mn2:17.1: If he did not use them, influxes causing affliction and vexation would arise; but using them, those influxes causing affliction and vexation do not arise.
mn2:17.2: These, monks, are called the influxes to be abandoned by use.
mn2:18.0: 4. Influxes to Be Abandoned by Endurance
mn2:18.1: And what, monks, are the influxes to be abandoned by endurance?
mn2:18.2: Here, monks, a monk, reflecting wisely, is patient with cold, heat, hunger, and thirst; with contact with flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping creatures; with abusive and hurtful speech; and with arisen bodily feelings that are painful, sharp, piercing, bitter, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-threatening—he is one who endures them.
mn2:18.3: If he did not endure them, influxes causing affliction and vexation would arise; but enduring them, those influxes causing affliction and vexation do not arise.
mn2:18.4: These, monks, are called the influxes to be abandoned by endurance.
mn2:19.0: 5. Influxes to Be Abandoned by Avoidance
mn2:19.1: And what, monks, are the influxes to be abandoned by avoidance?
mn2:19.2: Here, monks, a monk, reflecting wisely, avoids a fierce elephant, a fierce horse, a fierce bull, a fierce dog, a snake, a stump, a thorny place, a pit, a precipice, a sewer, or a cesspool.
mn2:19.3: He avoids sitting in unsuitable seats, wandering in unsuitable places, and associating with bad friends, as wise fellow practitioners might suspect him of evil conduct in such cases, and so he avoids those unsuitable seats, unsuitable places, and bad friends, reflecting wisely.
mn2:19.4: If he did not avoid them, influxes causing affliction and vexation would arise; but avoiding them, those influxes causing affliction and vexation do not arise.
mn2:19.5: These, monks, are called the influxes to be abandoned by avoidance.
mn2:20.0: 6. Influxes to Be Abandoned by Removal
mn2:20.1: And what, monks, are the influxes to be abandoned by removal?
mn2:20.2: Here, monks, a monk, reflecting wisely, does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire—he abandons it, removes it, eliminates it, and makes it cease; he does not tolerate an arisen thought of ill will … an arisen thought of harming … or any arisen evil, unwholesome states—he abandons them, removes them, eliminates them, and makes them cease.
mn2:20.3: If he did not remove them, influxes causing affliction and vexation would arise; but removing them, those influxes causing affliction and vexation do not arise.
mn2:20.4: These, monks, are called the influxes to be abandoned by removal.
mn2:21.0: 7. Influxes to Be Abandoned by Development
mn2:21.1: And what, monks, are the influxes to be abandoned by development?
mn2:21.2: Here, monks, a monk, reflecting wisely, develops the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, dependent on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in release;
mn2:21.3: he develops the investigation-of-states factor of enlightenment …
mn2:21.8: the equanimity factor of enlightenment, dependent on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in release.
mn2:21.9: If he did not develop them, influxes causing affliction and vexation would arise; but developing them, those influxes causing affliction and vexation do not arise.
mn2:21.10: These, monks, are called the influxes to be abandoned by development.
mn2:22.1: When, monks, a monk has abandoned by seeing the influxes to be abandoned by seeing, abandoned by restraint the influxes to be abandoned by restraint, abandoned by use the influxes to be abandoned by use, abandoned by endurance the influxes to be abandoned by endurance, abandoned by avoidance the influxes to be abandoned by avoidance, abandoned by removal the influxes to be abandoned by removal, and abandoned by development the influxes to be abandoned by development;
mn2:22.2: this, monks, is called: ‘A monk dwells restrained with the restraint of all influxes, has cut off craving, undone the fetters, and by fully understanding conceit, has made an end of suffering.’
mn2:22.3: This is what the Blessed One said.
mn2:22.4: The monks, delighted, rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
mn2:22.5: The All Influxes Discourse, second, is concluded.
